body.p: In view of the claim amendments and below remarks, the Examiner is respectfully requested to reconsider the rejections. The Applicant thanks the Examiner for the determination of allowable subject matter.
Office Action Summary
Claims 17, 25 and 26 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph, as failing to comply with the written description requirement.
Claims 22 and 34 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite.

Claims 16-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian et al., (US20170097413A1) in view of Griesdorf et al., (US9989622B1) and in further view of Stivoric et al., (US20170156594A1).

Claim 21 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf and Stivoric as applied to claim 18 above, and further in view of Hauenstein et al., (US20170095181 A1), (hereinafter "Hauenstein").

Claim 23 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf and Stivoric as applied to claim 18 above, and further in view of Sun et al., (US20120203491A1) (hereinafter "Sun") and Komaromi et al., (US20160162256A1) (hereinafter "Komaromi").

Claim 24 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf and Stivoric as applied to claim 16 above, and further in view of Alsheikh et al. (M. A. Alsheikh, S. Lin, D. Niyato and H. -P. Tan, "Machine Learning in Wireless Sensor Networks: Algorithms, Strategies, and Applications," in IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials, vol. 16, no. 4, pp. 1996-2018, Fourth quarter 2014, doi: 10.1 109/COMST.2014.2320099) and Simpson et al., (US20190336107A1).

Claim 25 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf and Stivoric as applied to claim 20 above, and further in view Kim et al., "Tracking a Moving Target with Multipole Doppler Sensors Using an Artificial Neural Network", IEEE Antennas and Propagation Society International Symposium, June 9-15, pp. 1477-1480, (hereinafter "Kim") and Rogers, (US20170351827A1) (hereinafter "Rogers").
Claim 26 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf and Stivoric as applied to claim 17 above, and further in view of Sun and Komaromi.
Claims 27-30 and 34 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian in view of Griesdorf and Stivoric.
Claim 31 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf and Stivoric as applied to claim 29 above, and further in view of Rogers.
Claim 32 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, and Rodgers applied to claim 31 above, and further in view of Hauenstein,

Claim 33 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, Rodgers, and Hauenstein applied to claim 32 above, and further in view of DeLuca et al., (US6238338B1).
Claim 35 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian in view of Griesdorf and Stivoric.

Claim 22 would be allowable if rewritten to overcome the rejection(s) under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), 2nd paragraph, set forth in the Office action and to include all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.

Claim 17 is amended in accordance with the Examiner's remarks on page 3 of the Office Action. Support for the amendment to claim 17 is within the filed specification at page 4, lines 11-14 and page 4, lines 23-26.

Claim 22 is amended to clarify that the docking and charging are two options that may be performed individually (docking or charging but not both) or simultaneously (docking and charging). The wherein clauses indicate that 1) when the first apparatus is docking the second apparatus, the first apparatus provides the pseudo sensor data, and that 2) when the first apparatus is charging the second apparatus, the first apparatus provides the pseudo sensor data. Support for the amendment to claim 22 is within the filed specification at page 8, lines 19-22, page 11, lines 35-38, page 12, line 37 to page 13, line 2, and FIG. 4.

Claim 34 is amended to clarify that the apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker can receive from the another apparatus comprising the application an indication to track the user. The apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker provides the pseudo sensor data in response to receiving from the another apparatus comprising the application the indication to track the user. Support for the amendment to claim 34 is found within the filed specification at page 11, line 38 to page 12, line 2.
For the foregoing reasons, the Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw the rejections based on Section 112.

The Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw the rejections based on Section 103, because the prior art does not disclose or suggest the subject matter of the independent claims. MPEP 2143.03 (all claim limitations must be considered).
1. Independent claims 16, 27, 35: the prior art does not disclose or suggest a second apparatus comprising an application that processes pseudo sensor data
Independent claim 16 has been amended to claim:
"providing, using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker,

the pseudo sensor data derived based on at least the machine learning model to a second apparatus comprising an application to enable the application to process the pseudo sensor data and native sensor data to enable tracking the activity of the user, wherein the first apparatus is different from the second apparatus, and the first apparatus is configured to be
separate from the second apparatus;
wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived and provided to the second apparatus

using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user is not provided using the second apparatus comprising the application or is unavailable with the second apparatus
comprising the application."
Independent claims 27 and 35 have been amended similarly.
Support for this amendment is found within the filed specification at page 7, lines 27-30, FIG. 1, and FIG. 3B.

Griesdorf Fig. lA (corresponding to Fig. IA of Griesdorfs priority application, namely US provisional application number 62/474,414 filed March 16, 2017, hereinafter "Griesdorfs provisional") shows a wireless communication device 102C, where the " wireless communication device 102C may receive the wireless signals transmitted by the wireless communication devices 102A, 102B." Refer to Griesdorf column 6, lines 12-15.

Griesdorf column 6, lines 19-25 (corresponding to paragraph [0027] of Greisdorfs provisional) describes "In the example shown, the wireless communication device 102C, operating in a state defined by modem parameters, processes the wireless signals from the wireless communication devices 102A, 102B and detects motion of an object in a space accessed by the wireless signals. For example, the wireless communication device 102C may perform the example process 400 of FIGS. 4A-4C, or another type of process for detecting motion."

The Examiner stated on page 7 of the Office Action, regarding claim 16, that Griesdorf at the above referenced excerpts (Fig. 1A, column 6, lines 19-25) describes a second apparatus comprising an application, the first apparatus being different from the second apparatus, and the first apparatus being separate from the second apparatus. The Examiner applies the same rationale to reject the corresponding aspects of claim 27 (Office Action, pages 20-21) and claim 35 (Office Action, pages 27-28).
However, Griesdorf does not disclose or suggest a second apparatus comprising an
application that processes pseudo sensor data.
This is because the wireless communication device 102C 1) does not comprise an application, and 2) does not comprise an application that processes pseudo sensor data.

The wireless communication device 102C merely processes the wireless signals from the wireless communication devices 102A, 102B and detects motion of an object in a space accessed by the wireless signals. However, 1) the detecting of motion is not an application (as an application, or an app, is understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art), such as the health and fitness tracker application 390 as described by Applicant. Also, 2) the wireless communication device does not process pseudo sensor data, as the wireless communication device merely processes wireless signals from the wireless communication devices 102A, 102B.
Fig. 1 A of Griesdorf is shown below to illustrate:

Griesdorf's only mention of an "application" is at column 18, lines 37-38 describing an ASIC (application specific integrated circuit) and at column 18, lines 45-47 generally describing a computer program ("A computer program (also known as a program, software, software application, script, or code) can be written in any form of programming language").

In contrast, Applicant describes a second apparatus (health and fitness tracker 104) 1) comprising an application (application 390), where 2) the application processes pseudo sensor data. This is described within the Applicant's filed specification at page 7, lines 27-31 (bolding added): "the native sensor data in the form of, for example, accelerometer data 380A-B, 382A-B, and 384A-B along with the pseudo sensor data 390, 392, and 394 may be provided to an application 390, such as a health and fitness tracker application, to enable tracking the user's activity. The application 390 may, as noted above, be located at the health and fitness tracker 104."
This is shown using Applicant's FIG. 3B as illustrated below:

Accordingly, the prior art does not disclose or suggest a second apparatus comprising an application that processes pseudo sensor data to enable tracking activity of the user. Independent claim 16, on the other hand, claims (with similar aspects being recited in independent claims 27 and 35):
"providing, using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker,

the pseudo sensor data derived based on at least the machine learning model to a second apparatus comprising an application to enable the application to process the pseudo sensor data and native sensor data to enable tracking the activity of the user, wherein the first apparatus is different from the second apparatus, and the first apparatus is configured to be
separate from the second apparatus;
wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived and provided to the second apparatus

using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user is not provided using the second apparatus comprising the application or is unavailable with the second apparatus
comprising the application."
This is not disclosed or suggested in the prior art. Therefore, independent claims 16, 27, and 35 are patentable and should be allowed.

another apparatus comprising the application, an indication to track the user; and
provide, with the apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker to the
another apparatus comprising the application, the pseudo sensor data in response to receiving, with the apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker from the
Support for this amendment is found within Applicant's filed specification at page 11, line 38 to page 12, line 2.

Gillian paragraph [0069] describes "The detection features 512 may enable the sensor fusion engine 110 to detect a presence of a user, other people, or objects in an environment of the computing device 102. In some cases, a detection feature indicates a number of targets in a radar field or a number of targets in a room or space that is swept by a radar field. The reflection features 514 may indicate a profile of energy reflected by the target, such as reflected energy over time. This can be effective to enable velocity of a target's motion to be tracked over time. Alternately or additionally, the reflection feature may indicate an energy of a strongest component or a total energy of a moving target."
The Examiner stated on page 23 of the Office Action, regarding claim 34, that Gillian at the above-referenced excerpt ([0069]) describes that a target is tracked:
First, Gillian only describes one apparatus, namely computing device 102 that comprises the sensors 118, the radar sensor 120, and the sensor fusion engine 110. Refer to Gillian Fig. 1.
Second, because Gillian only describes one computing device 102, Gillian does not

describe the computing device 102 receiving from a second device an indication to track the user, or the computing device 102 providing pseudo sensor data to a second device in response to receiving from the second device the indication to track the user.

In Gillian, as shown in Fig. 5, the sensors 118 provide the sensor data 506 to sensor fusion engine 110, and the radar sensor 120 provides the radar data 508 to the sensor fusion engine 110. The sensor fusion engine 110 includes the detection features 512 and the reflection features 514 that track the target. However the sensor fusion engine 110 does not receive an indication from the sensors 118 or the radar sensor 120 to track the target. Even if the sensor fusion engine 110 did receive an indication from the sensors 118 or the radar sensor 120 to track the target, the sensors 118, the radar sensor 120, and the sensor fusion engine 110 are all within the same computing device 102.
Portions of Fig. 5 and Fig. 1 of Gillian are shown below to illustrate:

reflection features 514 does not receive an indication to track the user from a second device, as sensors 118, radar sensor 120, and sensor fusion engine 110 are all within the same computing device 102.

In contrast, Applicant describes that the RF based tracker 110 receives an indication from the health and fitness tracker 104 to track the user, and the RF based tracker 110 provides to the health and fitness tracker 104 the pseudo sensor data in response to receiving the indication from the health and fitness tracker 104 to track the user.

Applicant's filed specification describes this embodiment at page 11, line 38 to page 12, line 2: "Alternatively or additionally, the health and fitness tracker 104 may trigger the RF based tracker 110 to track the user in response to the health and fitness tracker 104 transmitting an indication, such as by transmitting a trigger signal or sending a message, to the RF based tracker 110."

the indication to track user 102. Such an embodiment is not disclosed or suggested by the prior art including Gillian.

Accordingly, the prior art does not disclose or suggest: receiving, with the apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker from the another apparatus comprising the application, an indication to track the user, and providing, with the apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker to the another apparatus comprising the application, the pseudo sensor data in response to receiving, with the apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker from the another apparatus comprising the application, the indication to track the user. Claim 34, on the other hand, claims "receive, with the apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker from the another apparatus comprising the application, an indication to track the user; and provide, with the apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker to the another apparatus comprising the application, the pseudo sensor data in response to receiving, with the apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker from the another apparatus comprising the application, the indication to track the user." This is not disclosed or suggested by the prior art. Therefore, dependent claim 34 is patentable for this additional reason and should be allowed.
3. Even if it was obvious to combine the references, they do not disclose or suggest all of the elements/features of the claims, as explained above
Applicant respectfully traverses the rationale to combine the references to support a rejection under Section 103.

For example, because Griesdorf does not disclose or suggest a second apparatus comprising an application that processes pseudo sensor data, one skilled in the art would not be motivated to combine Gillian with Griesdorf to arrive at Applicant's claimed invention. Griesdorf's only mention of an "application" is at column 18, lines 37-38 describing an ASIC (application specific integrated circuit) and at column 18, lines 45-47 generally describing a computer program ("A computer program (also known as a program, software, software application, script, or code) can be written in any form of programming language")
Further, Stivoric does not describe that when the sensor or accelerometer fails, a device associated with the sensor or accelerometer receives pseudo sensor data from another device.

Whereas in Applicant's case, when the user equipment 104 stops providing sensor data, the user equipment 104 receives the pseudo sensor data from the RF based tracker 110. Therefore, one skilled in the art would not be motivated to combine Gillian with Stivoric to arrive at Applicant's claimed invention.
Even if, for the sake of argument, it was obvious to combine the references, they do not disclose or suggest all of the elements/features of the claims, as explained above.
4. Other dependent cains

Though the other dependent claims contain their own allowable subject matter, these claims should at least be allowable due to their dependence from allowable independent claims. However, to expedite prosecution at this time, no further comment will be made.
Status Of Griesdorf As Prior Art

Because Griesdorf was published June 5, 2018 after Applicant's priority date of July 20, 2017, Griesdorf is only prior art under 35 U.S.C. § 102(d) to the extent that Griesdorf's provisional filed March 16, 2017 "describes the subject matter" of Applicant's invention. The Examiner is therefore respectfully requested to cite to Griesdorf's provisional rather than to Griesdorf in any subsequent Office Action.

The Applicant respectfully requests the Examiner enter this amendment and pass the claims to issue. The undersigned representative welcomes the opportunity to resolve any matters that may remain, formal or otherwise, via teleconference at the Examiner's discretion.
